dossier.summary: Harborview Construction is a commercial general contractor with about 120 people. It runs 15 to 20 projects at a time and works with more than 200 subcontractors.
dossier.why_now: Posted an opening for an accounts payable specialist last month.

stories.problem: Subcontractor invoices came in by mail and email to six project managers, and approvals sat on desks for weeks. Subs called the office every Friday asking when they would be paid.
stories.approach: Moved every invoice into one queue, matched each one to its purchase order, and sent approvals to project managers on their phones at the job site.
stories.result_metric: Days to approve a subcontractor invoice
stories.quote: Our PMs approve invoices from the job site now. Nobody chases paper on Friday afternoons anymore.

stories.problem: Invoices could not be paid until a signed lien waiver came back, and the waivers lived in a shared inbox. Payments ran late and vendors put jobs on hold.
stories.approach: Tied each lien waiver to its invoice, held payment until the waiver arrived, and sent the vendor a reminder when one was missing.
stories.quote: We stopped getting calls from suppliers threatening to pull crews. That alone was worth it.

size_matches.industry: transportation, logistics, supply chain and storage
size_matches.problem: Fuel, repair and toll invoices for a fleet of 90 trucks were keyed in by two people, and closing the month took nine working days.
size_matches.approach: Read fuel and repair invoices automatically, coded each one to the right truck, and sent only the exceptions to a person.
size_matches.result_metric: Working days to close the month
size_matches.quote: Close used to eat the first two weeks of every month. Now it is done before the first Friday.

size_matches.problem: Twenty-two offices ordered their own supplies, and the two-person AP team spent most of the week matching packing slips to invoices.
size_matches.approach: Each office took a photo of the packing slip on delivery, and invoices were matched against it automatically.
size_matches.result_metric: Hours a week spent on AP
size_matches.quote: My team gets to do finance work again instead of matching paper.

size_matches.problem: Software bills were spread across 40 company cards, and finance only heard about renewals after they were charged.
size_matches.approach: Pulled every vendor bill into one list with an owner and a renewal date, and flagged each renewal 30 days ahead.
size_matches.quote: We found three tools nobody had opened since spring.

size_matches.problem: Ingredient suppliers sent invoices by email, by mail and through portals, and the same invoice sometimes got paid twice.
size_matches.approach: Collected invoices from every channel in one place and checked each new invoice against everything already paid.
size_matches.quote: Every duplicate we paid was money we had to chase back. Now they never go out.

size_matches.problem: Contractor and vendor invoices piled up across nine branch offices, and late fees showed up on almost every statement.
size_matches.approach: Routed invoices from every branch to one approver and scheduled payments by due date instead of by when someone got to them.
size_matches.quote: Late fees were a line item we had stopped questioning. Now they are close to zero.

size_matches.problem: Maintenance vendors sent invoices for 60 buildings to property managers, who forwarded them to accounting when they had time.
size_matches.approach: Gave every building its own invoice inbox, coded invoices to the property automatically, and sent approvals to the right manager.
size_matches.result_metric: Days to approve a maintenance invoice
size_matches.quote: Our plumbers and electricians get paid on time, so they pick up when we call.

data.headline: How a builder your size cut invoice approvals from 19 days to 4
data.dek: Granite Ridge runs projects the way Harborview does, with a lot of subcontractors and project managers who live on site. Their invoice problem will sound familiar.
data.customer_about: A construction company with 51 to 200 people

parallel.label: Size
parallel.them: 51 to 200 people, running several projects at once.
parallel.you: About 120 people, running 15 to 20 projects at a time.

parallel.label: Who sends invoices
parallel.them: Subcontractors, sending invoices by mail and email to six project managers.
parallel.you: More than 200 subcontractors across your projects.

parallel.label: Who has to approve
parallel.them: Project managers who spend most of the day at the job site.
parallel.you: Project managers on 15 to 20 live projects, plus an AP role you are hiring for.

data.before: Subcontractor invoices came in by mail and by email, spread across six project managers. Approvals sat on desks for weeks. Every Friday the office fielded calls from subs asking when they would be paid.
data.after: They moved every invoice into one queue with us and matched each one to its purchase order. Approvals went to the project managers' phones, so a PM could sign off from the job site. Within three months, an invoice that used to wait 19 days was approved in 4.

result.metric: Days to approve a subcontractor invoice

quote.text: Our PMs approve invoices from the job site now. Nobody chases paper on Friday afternoons anymore.

data.fit: Harborview has the same shape as Granite Ridge: lots of subcontractors, project managers who are rarely at a desk, and approvals that depend on them. You are also hiring for AP, so this is a good moment to decide whether that role chases paper or does finance work. One difference: with more than 200 subs, your first month would go into setting up vendors, not approvals.
